name: Uma Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you talk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm growing manager on a vegetable farm that supplies two supermarkets: leeks, cabbages, cauliflowers and carrots, about 300 hectares. In the busy season I've got a picking crew of forty, and I'm out with them from six, checking quality, because if a lorry gets rejected at the depot, that's thousands lost. The rest of the year it's planting plans, irrigation and fighting with the weather.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a field done properly. Straight rows, clean leeks, the crew working well together. My grandad grew vegetables on this same road, Barrow Lane, and I like that I'm still doing it. And I like the crew. Some of them have come back every season for ten years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The supermarkets. They change the spec, the rules for size and shape, whenever they like, and we carry the cost. Pay's low for the responsibility. I'm getting married next summer to Tom, who works at the feed mill, and we've got a couple of weeks' money saved, most of which is meant for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, whatever helps. I don't use any of it myself. I'd not post about it, I'm not one for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means nothing for me, and I'm glad. I've got enough to learn without some computer program. My problems are the supermarket specs, the weather and finding enough pickers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on the same. Keep Tom and me saving for the wedding, maybe pick up a few Saturday shifts at the packhouse in winter. I'd let the office use whatever programs they like, as long as nobody makes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned finding enough pickers. How hard is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every year harder. Local people mostly won't do it. They'd rather sit at home, some of them, which I don't understand. Most of the crew come from abroad for the season, and the paperwork for that gets worse every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who makes that paperwork worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Government. Every year another form, another rule. I'd rather they let farmers get on with it. The supermarkets make enough rules without the government adding more.

S0.say: I'd say fine, whatever helps. I don't use any of it myself, and I'm not one for posting about it.
S0.think: It means nothing for me, and I'm glad. My problems are the supermarket specs, the weather and finding enough pickers.
S0.do: Carries on as usual, saving with her fiancé for the wedding and maybe picking up winter Saturday shifts at the packhouse. Lets the office use whatever software it likes as long as she isn't made to.
S0.feel: Calm; it's the same as now.
S0.quote: I'd let the office use whatever programs they like, as long as nobody makes me.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is proud, direct and rooted in place, with family history on the same road. Her blame goes to government paperwork and supermarket rules, and to local people she thinks won't work. She avoids AI completely and sees no reason to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for young people if companies stop hiring beginners. I'd say bring back proper apprenticeships, learning on the job from someone who knows. That's how I learned, from Mr Brennan and my grandad, not from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it'll pass me by. Slow is fine for vegetables. Though if the supermarket buying office uses AI to set the specs, they'll get even pickier, and I'd be the one standing in a field explaining to forty people why we're binning good leeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it. I'd push Mr Brennan to take on a local school leaver as a trainee, and I'd teach them myself. Maybe I'd ask the vicar to mention it, because half the village goes to church and someone's son will need work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly irritated at the thought of more rules from the supermarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you ask the vicar rather than put up an advert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people trust the vicar. If he says the Brennans are decent people to work for, a mother listens. An advert on a website, nobody reads it, or the wrong sort answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the supermarket specs you'd actually want a machine to handle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd want the supermarket to stop changing them. Last year they changed the leek length two weeks before harvest. We had to retrain the whole crew on the knife cut in a day.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame for young people if firms stop hiring beginners. We should bring back proper apprenticeships, learning on the job from someone who knows.
S1.think: It'll mostly pass me by, since slow change suits vegetables. But if the supermarket uses AI to set specs, they'll get pickier, and I'll be explaining to the crew why we're binning good leeks.
S1.do: Keeps working as she does and pushes the owner to take on a local school leaver she'd train herself. Asks the vicar to spread the word among families at church.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, mostly irritated at the thought of more supermarket rules.
S1.quote: Last year they changed the leek length two weeks before harvest. We had to retrain the whole crew on the knife cut in a day.
S1.fieldNote: Her answer to every change is people she trusts: her grandad, the farm owner, the vicar. She dislikes online adverts as much as AI. The supermarket remains her main enemy, more than any technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people losing office jobs should be helped back into work, not paid to sit at home. There's work out here. I'd say it at church coffee and at Tom's family Sunday lunch, where everyone has an opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the politicians will make a mess of it either way. If they hand out money, it comes from people like us in taxes. If they don't, the village gets poorer. Tom's sister does accounts at the agricultural merchant, and I'd worry for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the Brennans we should offer picking work to laid-off locals, starting in spring. I'd put off buying a house for a few more years, though we're nowhere near one anyway. And I'd keep Tom's sister in mind for any paperwork job going on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Annoyed at the politicians more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would laid-off office workers actually do the picking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few, for a week. Then their backs go and they leave. I've seen it. My best pickers are a married couple from abroad who've come back eight years running. You can't train that kind of grit in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said help people back into work, not pay them to sit at home. What if there's no work for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then help them, I suppose. But as a loan, or a training place, not money for nothing. My grandad would say a man needs work to keep straight. I'd say a woman does too.

S2.say: I'd say people losing office jobs should be helped back into work, not paid to sit at home, because there's work out here. I'd say it at church coffee and at Sunday lunch with Tom's family.
S2.think: Politicians will make a mess of it either way: handouts come from our taxes, but doing nothing makes the village poorer. I'd worry for Tom's sister, who does accounts at the agricultural merchant.
S2.do: Suggests the owners offer spring picking work to laid-off locals. Puts off any thought of buying a house and keeps her future sister-in-law in mind for farm paperwork jobs.
S2.feel: Uneasy, more annoyed at politicians than scared.
S2.quote: My grandad would say a man needs work to keep straight. I'd say a woman does too.
S2.fieldNote: Her traditional view on work over handouts is firm but softens when I pushed on people who can't find work; she'd accept loans or training. She doubts office workers would last at picking. Her worry is personal and local, through her future sister-in-law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who get rich from this should put something back, but through their own giving and their communities, not just more tax. I'd say the government should keep its hands off farms. And I'd say thank God for physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm safe for now, and it's a relief. But booming house prices means Tom and I will rent forever. And all those newly unemployed professionals means the supermarket customers trade down, so the supermarkets squeeze us harder on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding small, the church and the village hall, no fancy venue. I'd ask the Brennans if there's a cottage on the farm we could rent. I'd keep my head down and make sure our rejection rate at the depot stays the lowest of their suppliers, so they keep us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. Grateful too, that I work with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Keeping the wedding small. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would cry. She's been planning it since I was eight. But Tom's sensible, he'd back me. We'd say the money's better in a deposit than a dance floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your rejection rate now, and how do you keep it low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Under two percent last year, the lowest the buyer has seen from us. I walk every row before the crew does, and I'm not soft about it. If a cabbage isn't right, it stays in the field.

S3.say: I'd say people who get rich from this should put something back through giving and their communities, not just more tax. The government should keep its hands off farms, and thank God for physical work.
S3.think: I'm safe for now and relieved. But booming house prices mean we'll rent forever, and as customers trade down, the supermarkets will squeeze us harder on price.
S3.do: Keeps the wedding small, with the church and village hall. Asks the owners about renting a farm cottage and keeps the depot rejection rate under two percent so the supermarket keeps them.
S3.feel: A little anxious and grateful to work with her hands.
S3.quote: We'd say the money's better in a deposit than a dance floor.
S3.fieldNote: She feels safe in her job but squeezed on housing and through the supermarket. Her answer is thrift and pride in quality, not politics. The low rejection rate is her badge of honour and her job security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots picking vegetables will never match a good crew, and I'd say it to anyone. I'd tell the supermarket buyers too, if they asked. They wouldn't ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'll come for exactly my kind of farm. Picking and packing is the biggest cost we have. If a robot can cut a leek and put it in a crate, the Brennans would be fools not to buy one, and the crew's gone. And a farm with no crew doesn't need a crew boss. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pray about it, honestly. Then I'd ask Mr Brennan what he's planning. I'd try to make myself the person who knows the crops so well the robots can't do without me: the planting, the timing, the soil. I won't learn computers, but I'll know more about leeks than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground's moving under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn computers. Even if that's what keeps your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how it sounds. I'd probably end up learning the little I had to, the buttons. But I won't pretend I'd like it, and I won't be good at it. Some other girl with a tablet would be better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the couple who've come back for eight years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to tell them myself, face to face, before the season. They've got a house half-built back home on what they earn here. That's the bit I couldn't stand, telling them.

S4.say: I'd say robots will never match a good picking crew, and I'd say it to anyone, including the supermarket buyers if they ever asked.
S4.think: They'll come for exactly my kind of farm, because picking and packing is our biggest cost. A farm with no crew doesn't need a crew boss, and that's me.
S4.do: Asks the owner what he's planning and makes herself indispensable on planting, timing and soil. Would learn only the bare minimum of the robot controls, and would tell the returning picker couple herself, face to face, before the season.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like the ground is moving under her.
S4.quote: A farm with no crew doesn't need a crew boss. That's me.
S4.fieldNote: The robot scenario hits her squarely, because her role is managing the picking crew. She turns to prayer and to deeper crop knowledge rather than technology, then admits she'd learn the buttons if forced. Her strongest feeling is about the couple building a house with their wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because they're aimed right at vegetable picking. What would help is the supermarkets paying a fair price so farms can afford to keep people. And the government getting out of the way so small farms aren't buried in forms. Not handouts. Just a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the crew. Everyone thinks of farms as one farmer and a tractor. Our farm is forty people in a field at six in the morning, and most of them aren't from here.

headlineQuote: They've got a house half-built back home on what they earn here. That's the bit I couldn't stand, telling them.
portrait: Uma Ziegler is 27 and grows vegetables for two supermarkets on the same road her grandad farmed, running a picking crew of forty, and she's saving to marry her fiancé Tom, who works at the feed mill. She's proud, blunt and churchgoing, and she trusts people she knows, like the farm owner and the vicar, over adverts or software. She blames supermarkets and government paperwork for her troubles and prefers work to handouts, though she softens when pushed. She feels safe through the office-job scenarios, but robots that can pick vegetables would remove the crew and with it her job. Her hardest thought is having to tell a returning couple from abroad that their work is gone.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because picking robots would replace her crew and with it her job as crew boss.
whatWouldHelp: Supermarkets paying a fair price so farms can keep people on, and less government paperwork for small farms; a fair chance, not handouts.
